title: RP2: Hard I2C is intolerant of clock stretching.
body:
This arose from [this forum thread](https://forum.micropython.org/viewtopic.php?f=21&t=11745). This [driver](https://github.com/micropython-IMU/micropython-bno055) for the Bosch BNO055 IMU has been tested on Pyboards, ESP32 and ESP8266 but has proved problematic on the Pico. Investigation showed that the IMU indulges in clock stretching for varying periods. The longest I have observed is 500μs.
### Hard I2C
Hard I2C, invoked as below, fails almost immediately with an EIO error.
```python
i2c = machine.I2C(0, sda=machine.Pin(16), scl=machine.Pin(17))
```
By contrast, hard I2C works on Pyboards and on ESP32.
### Soft I2C
On RP2 soft I2C must be invoked with a higher timeout value:
```python
i2c = machine.SoftI2C(sda=machine.Pin(16), scl=machine.Pin(17), timeout=100_000)
```
Subsidiary question. On ESP32 and ESP8266, soft I2C works with the default timeout. This now seems surprising.

Should the default timeout be increased?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> Hard I2C, invoked as below, fails almost immediately with an EIO error

Interesting!  It would be good to see if the rp2040 datasheet, or pico-sdk, says anything about clock stretching.



> Subsidiary question. On ESP32 and ESP8266, soft I2C works with the default timeout. This now seems surprising.

Yes that's surprising, because they share the same code with rp2.  I'm guessing it's the implementation of the delay, `mp_hal_delay_us_fast()`, that could be different, probably more accurate on rp2 (ie faster).

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Scrub my comments about SoftI2C on ESP32 and ESP8266. When I developed the driver soft I2C was specified with id==-1 and the I2C constructor did not have a timeout arg. The problem has emerged since the timeout was introduced in the SoftI2C constructor. IOW SoftI2C is consistent across all three platforms.

The I2C section of the RP2040 datasheet seems to have no reference to clock stretching. However it is discussed in their PIO implementation of I2C.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> The problem has emerged since the timeout was introduced in the SoftI2C constructor.

Maybe the default timeout needs to be increased?

> The I2C section of the RP2040 datasheet seems to have no reference to clock stretching

It does mention stretching when the RP2040 is in controller (master) mode.  But I also couldn't see any reference to peripheral clock stretching support.  I'd be surprised if it doesn't support it though.

This comment at CircuitPython seems to indicate that the BMO005 does work with the Pico: https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/issues/4082#issuecomment-776961617

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I don't think the issue is as the title says -- I think the peripheral can do clock stretching, but there are several other possibilities here:

1. There are many timing knobs in the I2C hardware. Some problems with some earlier timing values default values were fixed in https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/pull/314. If MicroPython is up-to-date on pico-sdk (I thought it was), then this should be fixed. But I am not sure what version of MicroPython the user in the original [forum thread](https://forum.micropython.org/viewtopic.php?f=21&t=11745) is using.

2. The RP2040 I2C hardware cannot do zero-length writes, which are often used for device scanning. So both MicroPython and CircuitPython and MicroPython both use bitbang I2C to do these writes. However, MicroPython does bitbang for writes up to length 2, and CircuitPython uses it only for zero-length writes:
https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/cf258c898eab664615220683d0f9e0507383b925/ports/rp2/machine_i2c.c#L130
So perhaps the simple clock-stretching for these writes is not good enough. Indeed, CircuitPython had the wrong clock stretch value for these writes initially, and we fixed it: https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/pull/4390.

3. The default clock speed for MicroPython is 400kHz, for CircuitPython it is 100kHz.


comments.author: reporter
participant1
comments.body:
> Why not choose the default value so that a t/o will only occur in the event of a hardware failure?

That would mean increasing it to a large value.  But too large means blocking for a while before you realise there's a failure, which could impact other things (eg in an asyncio based application).

That said, bumping it up so the BNO055 works out-of-the-box does seem like a sensible thing to do.

> While I like the logic of the patch I'm curious as to why it is needed. Why does bitbangio fail for transfers of length 1 or 2?

It could be because of the turn around of the GPIO configuration, changing it from alt-function (controlled by the I2C peripheral) to standard GPIO then back again.  This may put some transient signals on the lines that confuse the sensor.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
There could be clock-stretching needed for one- or two-byte writes on a particular (badly-behaved?) sensor, and that stretching would be limited to `.us_timeout = 255,`.

In fact we saw a very similar timeout problem with zero-byte writes for a new implementation of our seesaw protocol on an ATTiny. 255 was not quite long enough for it to respond. So we lengthened the zero-bytes timeout (to something too long -- it could be made shorter):
- https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/pull/5656

> This may put some transient signals on the lines that confuse the sensor.

I do not remember that I saw transients when I was debugging this  -- I think just saw hangups. I think I would I have gone to some effort to fix the transients if I had seen them. But I don't have any leftover screenshots.

The reason for the bitbang transaction is only because the I2C hardware does not handle zero-byte writes, so it may as well be used only in that case. Handling 1 and 2-byte writes that way was never really necessary, per https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/issues/238 and #6954. We found a problem with the bitbang 1- and 2-byte writes when debugging the TCS34725, a sensor that is even more badly behaved than the BNO055.

Here is the corresponding fix in CircuitPython to do only zero-byte writes with bitbang:
- https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/pull/4378

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I reduced the test script to this:
```python
import machine
import time
from bno055 import *

i2c = machine.I2C(0, sda=machine.Pin(16), scl=machine.Pin(17)) 
trig = machine.Pin(18, machine.Pin.OUT)
trig(0)

imu = BNO055(i2c)
count = 0
while True:
    time.sleep(0.1)
    try:
        print('Temperature {}°C'.format(imu.temperature()))
        count += 1
        print(count)
    except:
        trig(1)
        trig(0)
        print('FAIL')
        break
```
The call to `imu.temperature()` reduces to
```python
self._i2c.readfrom_mem_into(self.address, memaddr, buf)
```
which unpacks to:
```python
self._i2c.readfrom_mem_into(0x28, 0x34, bytearray(1))
```
As expected this fails. A normal transfer looks like this:  
![Image](https://github.com/micropython-IMU/micropython-bno055/raw/master/temp/good.png)
and a bad one:  
![Image](https://github.com/micropython-IMU/micropython-bno055/raw/master/temp/bad.png)
Zooming in on the second transfer - good:  
![Image](https://github.com/micropython-IMU/micropython-bno055/raw/master/temp/good_second_byte.png)
bad:  
![Image](https://github.com/micropython-IMU/micropython-bno055/raw/master/temp/bad_second_byte.png)
On a second run the protocol analyser produced a similar result, showing an erroneous 0x50 for the second transfer just before the exception and trigger occurs.

If you need to examine the data more closely I can publish the capture file. With the Saleae software (a [free download](https://www.saleae.com/downloads/)) the capture can be studied in detail.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Thanks for the traces.  For the "good", is that using `machine.SoftI2C`, or is it a case of `machine.I2C` that succeeds (I'm assuming the latter)?  What value for `.us_timeout` is it using, 255 or did you change the C code to 100000?

The `readfrom_mem_into` is a 1-byte write followed by a 1-byte read.  In the current firmware, when using `machine.I2C`, that will use software I2C for the 1-byte write, then hardware I2C for the 1-byte read.

The "bad" is failing in the 1-byte write.  It looks like the BNO055 stretches the clock for about 350us before it responds with ACK for the 0x28 address, and then the rp2040 sends 0x50 instead of 0x34... and I think the BNO NACKs that value, leading to an `OSError`.

After it failed I then rebooted and did another run to see if the "bad" transfer remained similar to the first. It was similar, notably the value 0x50.

Is it relevant that `0x50 == 0x28 << 1`?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I've examined the capture some more. After the address is sent, the clock stretching normally goes to a maximum of about 120μs. Prior to the failure the stretching is unusually long - 370μs on one run and 454μs on the other. This seems to confuse the bit banging driver.

The long delay seems to provoke the RP2 into re-sending the 0x28 address. The protocol analyser incorrectly interprets this as data, hence the observation of a value of 0x50 (because of the way the I2C address is left shifted to provide for the R/W bit). If the bit pattern is examined it looks like a repetition of address 0x28.

I haven't figured out how to interpret the transitions after the ACK, but these trigger the EIO exception as evidenced by the trigger pulse on pin 18.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
What's happening with the 0x50 is that the software I2C driver is doing a 0-byte write in order to release the bus cleanly after the timeout.

This is the sequence of calls:
- `.readmem_from_into(0x28, 0x34, bytearray(1))` at the Python level
- `machine_i2c_readfrom_mem_into`
- `read_mem`
- `mp_machine_i2c_writeto(self, 0x28, "\x34", 1, false)` - the `false` means do not send a stop condition at the end (because there will be a repeat start and read following it)
- this fails with ETIMEDOUT in `mp_hal_i2c_scl_release` while waiting for the ACK from the address (I'm guessing, by looking at the traces above)
- because of the above failure there's a call to do a 0-byte write to cleanly release the bus: `mp_machine_i2c_writeto(self, 0x28, NULL, 0, true)` - the `true` means send a stop

I can understand all the above (and the traces) if `us_timeout=255` because the BNO055 is stretching the ACK beyond that timeout value.  I don't understand why it would still fail in this way if `us_timeout=100000`.

@reporter are you certain that you tested it with `us_timeout=100000` as per https://github.com/micropython/micropython/issues/8167#issuecomment-1015262666?  Or even just `us_timeout=1000` should work.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Yes, I agree with that.

I think the SoftI2C default timeout should be increased substantially.

I take your point about blocking, but advanced users who care about this can override. A default which is too short leads to confusing, rare, errors. Further, while I have run the BNO055 for two hours with a SoftI2C timeout of 1ms, and I haven't measured clock stretching longer than 500μs, there is no way of knowing the worst-case. My tests were done with the IMU stationary. A timeout at 60,000 feet caused by the shock when the rocket first stage detaches would be embarrassing. Lastly, in a tested system, a true timeout (infinite clock stretching) should only occur if the attached hardware actually fails.

The blocking issue can always be highlighted in the docs.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Fixed by a707fe50b085ec83722106609f6fd219faf9f030

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I increased the default SoftI2C timeout to 50ms in 7d71ae25edc4b405dd03222f044bc7cf3b77f956.  50ms matches the existing timeout for stm32 hardware I2C.

> Lastly, in a tested system, a true timeout (infinite clock stretching) should only occur if the attached hardware actually fails.

Yes, but it than case you'd want the software to timeout as early as possible to catch the hardware failure, and then maybe do something about it :smile: 

I think 50ms is a fair value, it's 100x the 500us seen on the BNO055.  And for a broken I2C bus with SCL permanently low, an I2C.scan() takes about 5 seconds.

Users can do "non blocking" I2C scans by explicitly scanning each device with a 0-byte write, if needed.
